summary: Reviews earlier IAB statements on Internet transparency and discusses new issues. It argues that impeding network transparency, deliberately or not, harms the Internet's ability to support innovation and global communication, and gives illustrations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet works best when messages pass through without being blocked. This note explains why blocking and changing things in the middle can cause harm.

questions: why are application layer gateways a problem
why does dns answer rewriting break dnssec
subtitle: The IAB looks at what blocking, rewriting and steering traffic in the middle does to the Internet's openness.

tldr.problem: The Internet has grown while its transparency has shrunk, as filters, gateways and rewriting devices in the network interfere with traffic, and new technologies add fresh barriers.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB reaffirms the end-to-end principle and the idea of oblivious transport, then goes through application filtering, QoS, application layer gateways, IPv6 address limits, DNS tampering and load balancing, and asks providers to disclose any departure from transparency.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational statement, not a standard. Its message is that transparency, once lost, is hard to regain, and that restrictions are best applied at the edge with customer consent.

today: RFC 4924 is an Informational statement from the IAB. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Transparency and Oblivious Transport
sections.content:
A network that does not filter or transform the data it carries is called transparent or oblivious to the content of packets. The RFC argues this is the Internet's most essential characteristic, because new services can be deployed without changing the core. It quotes RFC 1958: the goal is connectivity, the tool is the Internet Protocol, and the intelligence is end to end.

The document reaffirms earlier IAB statements, including RFC 2775 and RFC 3724, describes the concept of oblivious transport from the DARPA NewArch project, and addresses new transparency issues that have appeared since.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of the postal service delivering letters without opening them. Because it does not care what is inside, anyone can invent a new kind of letter and it still gets there.

sections.title: The Tussle Over Transparency
sections.content:
The RFC admits that full transparency has a cost: it also makes it easier to deliver unwanted traffic, and unwanted traffic is increasingly cited as a reason to limit it. Followed to its conclusion, that leads to ever more complex barriers, and since transparency once lost is hard to regain, the result could be an Internet that is both insecure and not transparent. The alternative the RFC describes is more sophisticated host-based security.

It also describes a tussle between subscribers, vendors, providers and society at large. Developers want oblivious transport, providers want to block unwanted traffic early, vendors want to sell in-network value-added services, and society may want to block offensive material. No architectural fix satisfies everyone, but providers can tell subscribers what service they are really getting.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone wants something different from the mail system. Some want it left alone, some want bad mail stopped. The fair thing is to tell people honestly what the post office does to their mail.

sections.title: Filtering and Quality of Service
sections.content:
Filtering that blocks or restricts applications without customer consent reduces innovation. The RFC says it is better done at the edges (provider access routers, customer equipment or hosts) so customers choose what to block, and notes it is hard to make work because developers re-engineer protocols around filters. Many application protocols began to use HTTP as a transport after noticing that firewalls allow HTTP but drop unknown protocols.

It leans on RFC 4084, which defines "Full Internet Connectivity" and asks providers to disclose any blocking, restriction or redirection. QoS is treated the same way: classes such as default or lower effort can see more random loss, expedited forwarding can lose packets that exceed its bandwidth, and application-specific bandwidth limits are equivalent to blocking from the user's point of view. Customer-imposed limits, such as capping peer-to-peer file sharing, can be valid.
sections.plainLanguage: If a school blocks a game, kids will disguise it as homework. Blocking in the middle just makes things messier, and it is fairer to let each family choose its own rules.

sections.title: Gateways, IPv6 Addresses and DNS
sections.content:
Application Layer Gateways (ALGs), often built into NATs and firewalls, are a barrier because they must be updated for every new address-dependent application. The RFC says the difficulty is inherent in the design, so a "transparent ALG" is a contradiction in terms. DNS ALGs conflict with DNSSEC.

For IPv6, limiting address supply encourages NAT, which is a barrier to transparency. The RFC notes that the original policy suggested a /48 prefix for small sites and says a single /64 without prefix delegation would restrict addresses. It also describes IKEv2 gaps in assigning IPv6 prefixes.

On DNS, the RFC stresses that a unique root is essential, and objects to providers rewriting "name does not exist" answers into a Web page address. Such changes made between authoritative servers and stub resolvers cause DNSSEC validation failures.
sections.plainLanguage: A translator who rewrites everything you say gets in the way whenever you say something new. And if the phone book quietly lied when a name was missing, nobody could trust any page of it.

sections.title: Load Balancing and Redirection
sections.content: Techniques that send requests to different servers depending on where they come from can add value if well implemented, but can also reduce transparency or disrupt service. The RFC lists four cases: reverse NAT used to balance IPv6 servers hurts transparency; DNS redirection is based on the query source address, which may be a distant DNS server rather than the host; misconfigured filters can divert packets onto overlay networks where they are delayed or lost; and anycast needs careful planning to survive routing changes.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper who points visitors to the nearest shop can be great, but if the helper guesses wrong, people end up walking to the wrong town.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
NATs, transparent proxies and DNS namespace mangling weaken end-to-end security guarantees and get in the way of protocols that would strengthen them. The RFC quotes RFC 2775 on the "crunchy outside, soft inside" risk: once the boundary is breached, the whole intranet is open to trivial attack.

It adds that malware increasingly uses the application layer, which lessens the security value of barriers. Application restrictions, it says, are most flexibly imposed at the edge.
sections.plainLanguage: A hard shell with a soft middle, like an egg, is easy to ruin once cracked. Guarding each room is safer than only guarding the front door.
